passages.text: Review of the <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> (Cai, 1983) species group with the first conifer-feeding larva for Limacodidae and descriptions of two new species from China and Taiwan (Lepidoptera, Limacodidae)

Although the caterpillars are well-known for the stings and magnificent coloration, the systematics of Limacodidae is historically neglected and chaotic due to the difficulty in matching the larval with adult stages as well as the very conservative and convergent adult morphology. <sentence_start/>One of the biggest taxonomic problems surrounds a collective group from Southeastern Asia, termed the “green limacodid moths”, which harbours at least 90 species placed in the genus <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> Walker, 1859 and 14 “subunits”. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">P. undulata</italic> group was previously composed of 3 species from China and Taiwan, and characterized only by wing pattern. <sentence_start/>This species group is extensively studied herein with two new species described, i.e. <italic toggle="yes">P. viridiflamma</italic> <bold>sp. n.</bold> (Taiwan) and <italic toggle="yes">P. minwangi</italic> <bold>sp. n.</bold> (S. China), and discovery of female genitalia of three species, presenting new phylogenetic insights in this potentially paraphyletic genus. <sentence_start/>In addition, one limacodid larva was found to be feeding exclusively on <italic toggle="yes">Picea</italic> (Pinaceae) in Taiwan. <sentence_start/>Its identity, <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic> Solovyev, 2010 in <italic toggle="yes">P. undulata</italic> group, is confirmed through matching its COI sequence to the adult. <sentence_start/>This discovery is also biologically significant because the previous known host breadth of <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> was of polyphagy on various angiosperm plant families. <sentence_start/>This case, therefore, represents the first record of conifer-feeding behavior in this family as well as the first of specialized herbivory in the genus. <sentence_start/>Meanwhile, the background match between <italic toggle="yes">Picea</italic> leaves and larval coloration is shared with other <italic toggle="yes">Picea</italic>-feeding insects. <sentence_start/>This phenomenon is worth of further investigation in the aspect of convergent evolution of crypsis associated with a particular plant.
(1) Systematic problems surrounding the genus <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> Moore, 1859 and its relatives.

The southeastern Asian limacodid moths comprise about 90 species of “green limacodids”, that are green at least on some parts of wings and thorax (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Holloway 1986</citation>; <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1134/S0013873811010088" count="1">Solovyev 2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>These species were hitherto all embedded in the genera <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> Moore, 1859 (based on a New World species, <italic toggle="yes">Parasa chloris</italic> Herrich-Schäffer, [1854]) and <italic toggle="yes">Latoia</italic> Guérin-Ménéville, 1844 (based on a Madagascan species, <italic toggle="yes">Latoia albifrons</italic> Guérin-Ménéville, 1844) according to interpretation of morphology, including known female and immature characters (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Seitz 1913</citation>; <citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" count="1">van Eecke 1925</citation>; <citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Inoue et al. 1982</citation>, <citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1992</citation>; <citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Cai 1983</citation>; <citation rid="B32" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Wu and Fang 2009</citation>, <citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2010</citation>; <citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Wu 2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>The taxonomic history of these groups has been detailed in several studies, i.e. <citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Holloway (1986)</citation>, <citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Holloway et al. (1987)</citation> and <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1134/S0013873811010088" count="1">Solovyev (2011)</citation> and the current generic name <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> has been adopted and generally accepted for the Southeast Asian green limacodids since <citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Holloway (1986)</citation>.

Though a subgrouping of <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> into 14 subunits was proposed by <citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Solovyev and Witt (2009)</citation> and <citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Solovyev (2010</citation>, <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1134/S0013873811010088" count="1">2011</citation>) based on the diversity of wing color patterns and differences in genitalia, the potential paraphyly of this genus indicated by <citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Holloway (1986)</citation> has not yet been elucidated. <sentence_start/>This is mainly due to the conservative male genitalia, except in the <italic toggle="yes">Parasa bicolor</italic> species group, as well as limited taxon sampling of female and immature characters. <sentence_start/>Futhermore, the green pigmental appearance is not only present in <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Latoia</italic>, but also in nine more genera according to <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1134/S0013873811010088" count="1">Solovyev (2011)</citation>. <sentence_start/>In addition, the presence of four black dorsal patches at the posterior marginal scoli of the larva seems to be a potential synapomorphy for <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> (Holloway, 1986). <sentence_start/>The concatenation of morphological characters (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Holloway 1986</citation>) and molecular data (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1134/S0013873811010088" count="1">Solovyev 2011</citation>) are expected to illuminate taxonomic problems surrounding the genus <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic>.
(2) Discovery of conifer-feeding habits with unique larval morphology and two additional new species in the <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> species group.

Recently, a single limacodid larva was discovered on the conifer tree Taiwan Spruce (<italic toggle="yes">Picea morrisonicola</italic> Hayata, 1908, Pinaceae), at mid-elevation (ca. 2600 m) of the central mountain range of Taiwan. <sentence_start/>This presents unusual ground maculation and an external appearance similar to the stomatal band of conifer leaves that is described and discussed in detail below.

Since this larva failed to pupate successfully after the prepupal stage in an indoor rearing environment, we sequenced its mitochondrial COI for comparison to that of two other limacodid moths. <sentence_start/>These two moths, <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic> Solovyev, 2010 and <italic toggle="yes">Parasa martini</italic> Solovyev, 2010, only occur in mid to high elevation montane regions of Taiwan. <sentence_start/>These data deposited in Genbank ( , , ) reveal zero divergence between the collected larva and the adult of <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic>, but ca. 6.3% p-distance divergence to <italic toggle="yes">Parasa martini</italic>, thus confirming the identity of the first known conifer-feeding limacodid (although not unique among zygaenoids, e.g. <italic toggle="yes">Psycharium</italic> Herrich-Schäffer, 1856, Somabrachyidae feeds on <italic toggle="yes">Pinus</italic>: <citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Epstein et al. 1999</citation>). <sentence_start/>Accompanying our larval discovery, we also describe two additional montane species, <italic toggle="yes">Parasa viridiflamma</italic> sp. n.and <italic toggle="yes">Parasa minwangi</italic> sp. n. <sentence_start/>The above four moth species all belong to the <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> species group as defined by <citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Solovyev (2010</citation>, <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1134/S0013873811010088" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition, the female genitalia have been regarded as including important characters to separate the genus <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> and the Madagascan <italic toggle="yes">Latoia</italic>. <sentence_start/>In the present study, all females and the genitalia of Taiwanese species are described for the first time. <sentence_start/>These results provide new evidences to reassess the relationships between the species groups of <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> or the so-called “green limacodids” globally.
The studied specimens were examined in or borrowed from the following institutions and private collections:
Collection of Valentin A. Kalinin, Moscow
Taiwan Endemic Species Research Institute, Nantou
National Museum of Natural Science, Taichung
National Museum of Nature and Science, Tsukuba
Entomological Department, South China Agricultural University, Guangzhou
Insect collection of Taiwan Forestry Research Institute, Taipei

Genitalia were prepared following the general method described e.g. by <citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Holloway et al. (1987)</citation> with slight modification. <sentence_start/>After maceration of the abdomen in 10% KOH and subsequent cleaning, male genitalia were carefully removed from the abdomen and abdominal segments 1-8 were opened along the caudocephalic axis from the right side. <sentence_start/>Female genitalia were removed entirely from the abdomen, cleaned and mounted with the ventral side uppermost. <sentence_start/>All the chitinuous genital tubes, including bursae, derived from the genital openings were preserved. <sentence_start/>Genitalia and abdominal skins of both sexes were stained with pen ink (Pilot), preserved in 70% ethanol then transferred in 99.5% ethanol before mounting in Euparal on slides. <sentence_start/>Specimens were photographed using a Nikon D300 digital camera.

The terminology of wing patterns and genital structures follows that of <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1134/S0013873811010088" count="1">Solovyev (2011)</citation>, that of immature morphology follows <citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5479/si.00810282.582" count="1">Epstein (1996)</citation>.

Genomic DNA was extracted from fragments of adult legs and part of larval tissues using an ALS Tissue Genomic DNA Extraction Kit (Kaohsiung, Taiwan). <sentence_start/>A partial COI sequence was amplified by a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with a set of universal primers (LCO1490 and HC02198) (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7881515" count="1">Folmer et al. 1994</citation>). <sentence_start/>The PCR was initiated at 95°XC for 5 min, followed by 35 cycles at 95°C for 1 min, 40°C for 1 min, and 72°XC for 1 min, with a final extension at 72°XC for 7 min. <sentence_start/>The PCR products were separated by electrophoresis in 1.5% agarose gels and sequenced. <sentence_start/>The 636 nucleotide base pairs of high quality COI sequences were aligned using CLUSTALX 2.0.10 (<citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/25.24.4876" pmid="9396791" pmcid="PMC147148" count="1">Thompson et al. 1997</citation>). <sentence_start/>Pairwise genetic distances were calculated using MEGA 4.0.2 (<citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/molbev/msm092" pmid="17488738" count="1">Tamura et al. 2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Three newly sequenced COI data were deposited in the GenBank database (numbers mentioned above) ( ). <sentence_start/>The voucher specimens were preserved in the Insect collection of Taiwan Forestry Research Institute, Taipei, Taiwan.

The definition and diagnosis of the <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> species group given in <citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Solovyev (2010</citation>, <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1134/S0013873811010088" count="1">2011</citation>) regarded the median green patch as a likely apomorphic character. <sentence_start/>Here we re-define this group by following characters:

Forewing with median green patch surrounded by two white longitudinal stripes, i.e. a short basal stripe and another long one along outer margin of the patch (see Figs 1-9). <sentence_start/>Notes. <sentence_start/>The combined pattern of forewings of the resting moths is similar to the needle leaves and stomatal band of several conifer genera, e.g. <italic toggle="yes">Pinus</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">Tsuga</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Abies</italic> (Pinaceae), thus revealing a potentially adult adaptation to such a resting environment (see Figs 26, 27).
Corpus bursae with only one transverse signum (see Figs 20-25), rather than two in other species groups of the genus <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic>.

Mature larva, at least that of <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic>, with green ground coloration, white longitudinal stripes and without dorsal abdominal scolus structures. <sentence_start/>See description part of immature stage of <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic> in detail.

This species is endemic to Taiwan. <sentence_start/>The adults occur in May and mid June to late August in mid-elevation mountain areas (1400-2610 m). <sentence_start/>The fresh individuals appear earlier in the season. <sentence_start/>Possibly univoltine. <sentence_start/>Hostplant unknown.

The new species is named through the combination of <italic toggle="yes">viridis</italic> (green) and <italic toggle="yes">flamma</italic> (flame), according to its flame-shaped green median patch on forewing.

passages.text: This species represents the insular sister species of <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> from China. <sentence_start/>It can be easily distinguished from <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> by its broader forewing medial green patch and its longer coecum. <sentence_start/>The comparison of the female genitalia is given under the diagnosis of the preceding species.
The female and mature larva are described for the first time.

Head. <sentence_start/>Antennae filiform. <sentence_start/>Eyes black, round. <sentence_start/>Frons, vertex, labial palpi fringed with long, chestnut hair-like scales, 3rd labial palpal segment short.

Thorax. <sentence_start/>Thoracic segments green with chestnut dorsal stripe. <sentence_start/>Forewing ground coloration chestnut with large median green patch delimited externally by thin white line which is in turn lined by brown border; marginal scales ochreous. <sentence_start/>Hind wings chestnut, marginal scales ochreous.
Abdomen. <sentence_start/>Abdominal segments fringed with long chestnut hair-like scales.

Female genitalia (Figs 22-23). <sentence_start/>Apophyses elongated, length of anterior and posterior ones equal; ductus bursae long; corpus bursae small, about 3.5 times shorter than ductus bursae, signum saddle-shaped in transverse axis.

Mature instar (Figs 28-33). <sentence_start/>Body spindle-like, length 20 mm when fully extended. <sentence_start/>Legs very small, largely reduced. <sentence_start/>Prolegs fully absent; adhesive, sucker-like regions on abdomen present. <sentence_start/>Head and body ground coloration green; a pair of prominent conical dorsal scoli arising from the dorsal part of mesothorax and on the 9th abdominal segment, respectively, the remaining parts smooth. <sentence_start/>10 fresh red spots, circled by light blue ring, arranged longitudinally along mid-dorsum; two cream yellow subdorsal lines running parallel adjacent to the red spots; dorso-lateral, lateral and ventro-lateral lines wide; regions between subdorsal and dorso-lateral lines pale green; small subdorsal scoli, arising from mesothorax, metathorax and abdominal segment A2 to A8, orange, along on lateral lines and reduced as small scobinate patches; spiracles orange.

Two new COI sequences (identical) from adult male and mature larva, respectively, were deposited in the GenBank database ( , ).

<italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic> is endemic to Taiwan. <sentence_start/>The adults occur from mid August to early October in mid to high elevation mountains of central Taiwan (~2000-3000 m), where they match the distribution range of the presently known hostplant, <italic toggle="yes">Picea morrisonicola</italic> Hayata (Pinaceae). <sentence_start/>The single mature larva was taken in late May, the leaf flushing period of <italic toggle="yes">Picea morrisonicola</italic>. <sentence_start/>This observation suggests a univoltine life cycle for <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic> and the overwintering stage is inferred to be the egg. <sentence_start/>The patterns of the adult and mature larva are similar to the needle leaves of Pinaceae, especially the hostplant species. <sentence_start/>This potential evolutionary adaptation is detailed in results and discussion.

passages.text: This species is closely related to the allopatric species <italic toggle="yes">Parasa martini</italic> from Taiwan. <sentence_start/>Externally its forewing white stripes are more slender. <sentence_start/>In the male genitalia the aedeagus has a more slender coecum and bears a separated, sclerotized dorsal process at the apex, the latter structure being absent in other species of the same group.

Head. <sentence_start/>Antennae bipectinate in male, rami longer at basal part and gradually shortening to absent at 5/6 from base; filiform in female. <sentence_start/>Eyes black, round. <sentence_start/>Frons, vertex, labial palpi fringed with long, chestnut hair-like scales, 3rd labial palpal segment short.

Thorax. <sentence_start/>Thoracic segments green with chestnut dorsal stripe. <sentence_start/>Forewing ground coloration chestnut with ochreous stripe situated between vein R4 and R5 and a large median green patch delimited by slender white lines and subsequent wide brown border; marginal scales ochreous. <sentence_start/>Hind wings chestnut, marginal scales pale chestnut fringed with ochreous.
Abdomen. <sentence_start/>Abdominal segments fringed with long chestnut hair-like scales.

Male genitalia (Figs 16, 17). <sentence_start/>Uncus robust, wide with hook-like apex. <sentence_start/>Gnathos large, sclerotized, apically narrowed; juxta sclerotized with two lateral sides extending dorsally. <sentence_start/>Valva short, apex tongue-like. <sentence_start/>Aedeagus long in straight distal part and down-curved basal part, respectively, and with a distal sclerotized dorsal process.

This species is recorded only from mid-elevation (600-1400 m) of Nanling mountain areas, S. China. <sentence_start/>The adults occur in April, May, June, August and September. <sentence_start/>Possibly bivoltine. <sentence_start/>Hostplant unknown.
This species is dedicated to Dr. Min Wang (SCAU), who represents the main collector of most of the type material of this new species in Nanling mountain areas, S. China.

passages.text: This species is the allopatric sister-species of <italic toggle="yes">Parasa minwangi</italic> sp. n. from southern China. <sentence_start/>Their comparison is given under the diagnosis of the preceding species.
The female is described here for the first time.

Head. <sentence_start/>Antennae filiform. <sentence_start/>Eyes black, round. <sentence_start/>Frons, vertex, labial palpi fringed with long, chestnut hair-like scales, 3rd labial palpal segment short.
Thorax. <sentence_start/>Thoracic segments green with chestnut dorsal stripe.

Forewing ground coloration chestnut with ochreous stripe situated between vein R4 and R5 and one median longitudinal green patch delimited by white lines and subsequent wide brown border; marginal scales ochreous. <sentence_start/>Hind wings chestnut, anal margin and marginal scales ochreous.
Abdomen. <sentence_start/>Abdominal segments fringed with long chestnut hair-like scales.

Female genitalia (Figs 24, 25). <sentence_start/>Apophyses elongated, length of anterior and posterior ones equal; ductus bursae long; corpus bursae small, about 3.5 times shorter than ductus bursae, signum transverse, long with medial part more expanded.
A new COI sequence was deposited in the GenBank database ( ).

This species is endemic to Taiwan. <sentence_start/>The adults occur from late May to late June, mid and late July then mid August to mid September in mid-elevation mountain areas with primary vegetation (ca. 950-2223 m). <sentence_start/>Possibly bivoltine. <sentence_start/>Hostplant unknown.

The present study reports on the first record of a conifer-feeding limacodid moth on the Taiwan Spruce (<italic toggle="yes">Picea morrisonicola</italic>) in Taiwan, describing the specialised morphology of the last larval instar. <sentence_start/>The larval identity is confirmed through COI sequence (636 bp) comparison between <italic toggle="yes">Parasa martini</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic>. <sentence_start/>The sequences of adult and larval <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic> are identical but about 6.3% divergent to <italic toggle="yes">Parasa martini</italic>.

The conifer-feeder, <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic> (Taiwan), together with <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> (central and southern China), <italic toggle="yes">Parasa martini</italic> (Taiwan), and the newly described <italic toggle="yes">Parasa viridiflamma</italic> sp. n. and <italic toggle="yes">Parasa minwangi</italic> sp. n., form the <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> species group sensu <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1134/S0013873811010088" count="1">Solovyev (2011)</citation>. <sentence_start/>The female and genital structures of the Taiwanese species are firstly illustrated and described before discussing the phylogenetic affinity with congeneric species.

Previously known <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> larvae are mostly regarded as being polyphagous, often as agricultural pests on broad-leaved trees (<citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Robinson et al. 2001</citation>, <citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2002</citation>) and possess the potentially synapomorphic character of four black dorsal scolus patches on their posterior margin (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Holloway 1986</citation>). <sentence_start/>The presence of dorsal and dorsal-lateral scoli places them in the first limacodid group as defined by <citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Solovyev and Witt (2009</citation>: 40). <sentence_start/>In the present study, the first record of a conifer-feeding limacodid moth, <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic>, together with description of the particular morphology of the mature instar is reported. <sentence_start/>This finding does not likely represent an occasional circumstance of a much broader host plant repertoire since external patterns of the adult and mature larva of <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic> are similar to the needle leaves of Pinaceae species, especially that of its hostplant <italic toggle="yes">Picea morrisonicola</italic>, revealing the tight specialization of the larva at least on Pinaceae. <sentence_start/>Conifer-feeding macrolepidopteran species in temperate regions that have larval patterns matching those of their hostplants were also reported and illustrated in several studies, e.g. the Japanese <italic toggle="yes">Sphinx caliginea</italic> (Butler, 1877) (Sphingidae) (<citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Nakatomi 1987</citation>; <citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Miyata 2011</citation>), <italic toggle="yes">Alsophiloides acroama</italic> (Inoue, [1944]) (Geometridae) (<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Nakajima 2011</citation>), the northern American <italic toggle="yes">Lithophane lemmeri</italic> (Barnes & Benjamin, 1929), <italic toggle="yes">Xestia badicollis</italic> (Grote, 1873) and <italic toggle="yes">Feralia comstocki</italic> (Grote, 1874) (Noctuidae) (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Maier et al. 2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>This phenomenon is worth of further investigation in the aspect of convergent evolution of crypsis associated with a group of particular plants.

Additionally, the larval habits of <italic toggle="yes">Parasa pygmy</italic> are also interesting. <sentence_start/>The observed larva always moves and feeds on the ventral side of needle leaf and branches, thus, its patterns and behavior can be regarded as a case of countershaded crypsis on Pinaceae to prevent predation by high mountain birds (lizard species occur more rarely in this high altitude biotope of Taiwan). <sentence_start/>Although it is cryptic, the prominent red spots of the mid-dorsal line of the mature larva, in contrast to its green ground coloration, act as a potentially aposematic signal (a similar pattern occurs in some <italic toggle="yes">Pinus</italic> feeding Bombycoidea, such as <italic toggle="yes">Lapara bombycoides</italic> Walker, 1856, Sphingidae). <sentence_start/>The combination of visual crypsis and aposematism was reported in previous studies, e.g. <citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Edmunds (1974)</citation>, <citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Rothschild (1975)</citation>, <citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Papageorgis (1975)</citation>, <citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/978-1-4615-6956-5_5" count="1">Endler (1978)</citation>; <citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198528609.001.0001" count="1">Ruxton et al. (2004)</citation>; <citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1098/rspb.2005.3079" pmcid="PMC1560331" pmid="16006332" count="1">Tullberg et al. (2005)</citation> and <citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.anbehav.2009.04.015" count="1">Gamberale-Stille et al. (2009)</citation>, and this kind of function can be modulated according to the distance between prey (signal) and predator (observer).

In addition to the descriptions of new species and the discovery of conifer-feeding larval habits, the female of three representatives of the <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> species group in Taiwan are reported for the first time. <sentence_start/>Their genitalia are different to those of other <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> species groups by the presence of only one signum rather than two. <sentence_start/>The number of signa is hitherto regarded as a significant character state to distinguish a broad sense pantropical <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> from Madagascan <italic toggle="yes">Latoia</italic>. <sentence_start/>The latter has no signum.

Though the known immature and female characters of the <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> species group show remarkable differences compared to the other <italic toggle="yes">Parasa</italic> species groups, the characters of wing venation and male genitalia are typical for the genus. <sentence_start/>Therefore, we hesitate to treat this lineage as an independent taxonomic unit until the mentioned characters can be comprehensively analyzed in all green limacodid groups.

In addition, the species richness and distribution of the <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> species group is extensively reviewed in this study, comprising wide-distributed <italic toggle="yes">Parasa undulata</italic> and local-ranged <italic toggle="yes">Parasa minwangi</italic> sp. n. in Asian continental region (China) and three endemic species found in a mountainous island (Taiwan). <sentence_start/>Assuming that no more or a few undescribed species may be discovered in the mainland in future studies, their distribution patterns show a rather higher species diversification in a small biogeographic unit. <sentence_start/>Though <citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1095-8312.1979.tb00036.x" count="1">Holloway and Hebert (1979)</citation> claimed the lower opportunities for specialization of conifer-feeding lepidopteran larvae compared to angiosperm-feeding ones, the hostplant selection of different conifer genera is still regarded as a potential key to speciation of this lineage which would be interesting to further investigate.
